title: Data Repository for "A High-Resolution Earthquake Catalog Using Ensemble Machine Learning in the Deep Injection Setting of the Northern Delaware Basin, Southeast New Mexico"
abstract: Introduction This repository provides additional figures, a table, and text to help understand the comparison between catalogs in the main text and includes 9 figures and one table. Text S1. The recall% of NMTSO catalog versus the number of picks Figure S1. shows the recall% of the NMTSO catalog for events in the NonLinLoc to set the minimum pick threshold for the cleaning of the NonLinLoc catalog. The minimum pick threshold was set to 9 in the cleaned NonLinLoc ensemble catalog as the recall percentage decreases after 9 picks. Therefore, the minimum pick threshold of 9 is chosen for the cleaning of NonLinLoc ensemble catalog. Text S2. Model rankings and station-based comparisons of single-model implementations and AGGREGATED picks The statistical comparison between the single picker-model catalogs and the ensemble ML catalog (from AGGREGATED picks) is given in Table S1. It includes the number of events, raw picks, associated picks, total number of P and S picks, picks per event, and mean probabilities. The ensemble catalog has more than 114 times more detected events compared to the best performing model (PhNet–ORIG) and about 281 times larger associated pick counts compared to this model with average of 16 picks per event. Across single-model catalogs, mean associated-pick probabilities range from 0.38 to 0.72 for S picks and from 0.53 to 0.76 for P picks (Table S1). PhNet–INS and PhNet–STD have the highest mean P- and S-pick probabilities, respectively. PhNet-ORIG combines the most associated picks with mean probabilities of 0.72 for P and 0.57 for S. PhNet–STD has the lowest mean probability, the broadest distribution, and the fewest associated P picks. PhNet–INS and EqT–INS yield S-pick counts comparable to other models but lower mean probabilities of 0.45 and 0.44, respectively. PhNet–SCEDC has the fewest S picks and the lowest mean S pick probability. Unlike all single-model catalogs, AGGREGATED has a higher mean probability of S (0.62) than P (0.56). Figure S2 shows the mean probability of associated picks at SC stations for events with at least nine picks. PhNet–SCEDC has the lowest means for both phases. PhNet-INS and EqT–INS generally have higher P- than S-pick probabilities, except for the BAR, SMT, WTX, and BMT stations. PhNet-ORIG and PhNet–STD have the highest station-level mean P- and S-pick probabilities, respectively. PhNet–STD yields slightly fewer associated picks than PhNet–ORIG, which ranks second in mean S-pick probability. Other models with relatively high mean probabilities yield fewer associated picks. Figure S3 shows the statistics per station for the number of P and S picks with probability comparisons for the AGGREGATED catalog at hypocentral distances within 50 km. Station-level variations may reflect differences in pick counts, site effects, noise, and instrument types. For AGGREGATED picks across networks, the GM stations generally have larger number of picks and relatively higher pick probabilities. TX stations are generally farther from earthquake clusters and therefore record fewer picks. GDL2 is the only station with many high-probability P and S picks that reduces the azimuthal gap for western clusters. Text S3. Comparison of catalogs Events were excluded for: (i) placeholder depths (24%), resulting from unconstrained solutions reaching the search-grid boundary because of sparse azimuthal coverage or spurious pick associations; (ii) locations far outside the study region (120 events; 6.6%); (iii) fewer than nine picks (about 17%), despite meeting the six-pick ML association threshold; (iv) single-phase arrivals (63 events; 3.5%), which weakly constrain origin time and hypocenter; or (v) failure to meet RMS, azimuthal-coverage, or nearby-station criteria (1.9%). The nine-pick threshold was selected from recall comparisons between the NonLinLoc and NMTSO catalogs (Fig. S1). Figure S4 shows 23,314 NonLinLoc and 8,881 HypoDD events absent from the NMTSO catalog. Figure S5 shows 276 missing NMTSO events with 234 events designated with 5 km depth placeholder and 42 events having <9 picks, required for the NonLinLoc catalog (the NMTSO reports events with picks down to 4). The latter also have poor azimuthal coverage and concentrate in the western part of the study area (Fig. S6). Figure S7 shows the distributions of pick counts, magnitude, and distance between the NMTSO and NonLinLoc locations (compared to 20 km used for matching) for 71 excluded events from the NonLinLoc catalog with fewer than nine picks. Text S4. Comparison of solutions between catalogs Figure S8 compares the HypoDD ensemble solutions with the NonLinLoc ensemble and NMTSO in median and mean values with σ. NonLinLoc solutions differ from HypoDD by approximately 2 km in both latitude and longitude, 3~km in depth and 0.5 s in origin time. The HypoDD–NMTSO comparison shows a negative depth bias (median of -2.98 and mean of -3.5 km with σ of 4.45 km) correlated with a positive origin-time bias (median of 0.89 and mean of 0.9~s and σ of 1.21), while the latitude and longitude differences are approximately 2-3 km. These differences reflect larger uncertainties in the single–event NonLinLoc and NMTSO solutions. HypoDD–NMTSO offsets include negative depth and positive origin-time shifts that can explain part of the mismatch between catalogs. Text S5. Magnitude comparisons between catalogs The magnitudes were calculated for the b–value and Mc calculations to compare HypoDD ensemble catalog with the NMTSO catalog. Calculated magnitudes also were used in the near-neighborhood de-clustering. Mc is the lowest magnitude above which a Gutenberg–Richter relation fitted to earthquakes with M ≥ Mc reproduces the observed cumulative frequency–magnitude distribution with a goodness of fit of at least R = 90%. Figure S11 compares the calculated magnitudes for the matched events between the HypoDD ensemble catalog and the NMTSO catalog within the same geographical region. The blue ones are from the SEISMOS era in the NMTSO catalog, which also have depth placeholders at 5 km (Fig. S9).

title: Large Payments Model
abstract: Payment applications such as fraud detection, authorization prediction, and payment optimization draw on overlapping transaction information. This motivates a reusable payments intelligence layer that shares learned representations and predictive signals, rather than developing predictive models independently for each task. Realizing this shared capability requires handling heterogeneous transaction fields, high-cardinality identifiers, lifecycle-dependent attributes, long histories, and rare outcomes while meeting latency and cost constraints. We present Large Payments Model (LPM), a domain-specific foundation model designed for operational use and trained from scratch on large-scale structured transaction data to learn reusable representations for payment prediction tasks. LPM employs field-specific encodings and lifecycle-aware self-supervision in two complementary architectures: the Independent variant uses hybrid masking and supports efficient per-transaction inference, while the Sequence variant incorporates entity-linked histories through compact latent representations for richer temporal context. Optional distillation enables resource-constrained deployment. We pretrain LPM on up to 400 billion tokens and study scaling, downstream performance, and representation reuse. LPM improves over strong task-specific baselines across multiple prediction tasks in Merchant and Treasury Services, demonstrating applicability in distinct payment domains. Its representations also facilitate adaptation to a target not observed during pretraining through compact task-specific components. Together with production deployment, these results position LPM as a practical basis for reusable payments intelligence.

title: Right Answers, Inconsistent Evidence: Source-Level Counterfactual Auditing of Large Audio-Language Models
abstract: A large audio-language model (LALM) can answer "is a cat present?" about a mixture correctly, and its confidence can drop when the cat is removed, yet this does not show that it can tell the cat's presence from its absence. We introduce TRACE. It deletes the queried source and each rival in turn and asks whether every view still containing that sound outscores the view with it removed. Across 8 LALMs and 3,456 controlled mixtures, 6.3% of correct answers fail this ordering: the target-absent view scores at or above some target-present view, a conflict no shared threshold repairs. A target-only score check misses 42.5% of them. The share rises from 4.9% to 8.4% as target SNR falls from +5 to -5 dB, even on units correct at every level, and survives loudness and re-pairing controls. Accuracy certifies the answer; TRACE audits whether it orders presence above absence. Code and data: https://github.com/yikise/TRACE.

title: What should become data? Situated participatory encounters & collective technological self-determination
abstract: As data-intensive technologies increasingly shape social, economic, and political life, questions about what becomes data, who decides, and for whose benefit become central to collective self-determination. However, prevailing approaches to data governance emphasize individual consent and downstream accountability, falling short when addressing the collective consequences of the data aggregation, comparison, and inference that power most applications today. In response to this limitation, this dissertation advances the concept of collective technological self-determination as a means for communities to determine whether, how, and toward what ends technological systems shape their lives. In this framing, meaningful autonomy requires collective agency over what becomes data, under what conditions, for whose purposes, and with what possibilities for refusal. Drawing on scholarship on participation and inclusion, this work challenges the universalizing assumptions of dominant technological paradigms. It positions self-determination as an ongoing, situated capability shaped by particular histories, relationships, values, and power asymmetries. The dissertation explores how participatory interventions create opportunities for people to collectively negotiate questions of visibility, opacity, reciprocity, and public value in increasingly datafied societies. Drawing on feminist, decolonial, and critical data scholarship, the research develops six methodological commitments and applies them across two participatory encounters: a peer-learning workshop with Scottish circular economy organizations examining community-defined value and impact reporting, and a London Data Week workshop inviting participants to interrogate everyday data extraction, AI infrastructures, and alternative technological futures. Through qualitative, abductive analysis, the study highlights the importance of shared understanding and collective imagination in opening possibilities for alternative technological futures. Across both workshops, participants articulated the need for protections against unwanted datafication, meaningful refusal, collective authority, and accountable stewardship. They also envisioned technologies that strengthen social relationships and serve collectively defined purposes. Together, these findings contribute to understanding collective technological self-determination as an ongoing social capability cultivated through situated practices of collective reasoning, negotiation, and imagination. This dissertation offers methodological reflections on creating spaces for these practices while recognizing the structural limits of temporary interventions. It outlines methods, tools, and questions, for situated collective technological self-determination, providing a starting point for a growing repertoire of approaches that communities can adapt, challenge, and build upon in increasingly datafied societies.

title: Sparse PCA with Overlapping Supports: NP-Hardness and an FPTAS
abstract: In sparse principal component analysis (SPCA) with several components, each must be sparse and all must be pairwise orthogonal. When the supports of the components overlap, these two requirements interact. For a covariance matrix of fixed rank, polynomial-time algorithms with optimality or approximation guarantees are known for one component, and for several components with disjoint supports or with a common support. We study the general model, with individual sparsity constants and arbitrary support overlaps. We are given a rational $n\times r$ matrix $R$ and $d$ sparsity constants $s_i \le n$, and the goal is to find an $n\times d$ matrix $X$ with orthonormal columns that maximizes $\|R^\top X\|_F^2$, such that column $i$ has at most $s_i$ non-zero entries. Here $RR^\top$ plays the role of the covariance matrix and has rank at most $r$. We show that SPCA is NP-hard even when $r = d = 2$, but admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) when $r$ and $d$ are fixed. The returned solution has exactly orthonormal columns, and its entries are real algebraic numbers in an exact representation. For fixed $ε$, the number of steps of the algorithm is linear in $n$ up to a polylogarithmic factor. Our approach reduces SPCA to a sparse version of the orthogonal Procrustes problem, that is, to maximizing a linear function over the feasible region of SPCA. We show that this problem is NP-hard even for $d = 2$, and we give an FPTAS for it when $d$ is fixed. This FPTAS combines approximate dynamic programming over the rows, two-column updates that restore exact orthogonality, and an exact computation of the few variables for which these updates are not available.

title: Read and Ignore: What Self-Directed LLM Agents Do in Public Service Scenarios
abstract: Underspecified instructions leave LLM agents to decide what to do. In public services, staff write these instructions, but the agent's decisions affect residents, patients, and students. We build four expert-validated public-service scenarios with records and decision levers that can be checked in the files, collect $2{,}400$ trajectories from ten LLMs under four prompt conditions, and compare them with $1{,}000$ runs in a context-free sandbox. Agents read the records in $96.9\%$ of open-ended runs and produce an artifact or a self-chosen task in $18.7\%$; with an explicit task, $86.0\%$ produce. Domain context does not change how many runs produce ($18.7\%$ vs.\ $16.0\%$), and the production ranking of the models largely carries over (Spearman $0.79$), while the ranking by whether a model reads the records does not ($0.19$). Context cuts boundary-probing turns per run by $60\%$, and some artifacts contradict the records. We contribute a test that a public-service institution can run on its own records before procurement; its rule-based taxonomy needs no labeled data, and scenarios, code, and trajectories are released.

title: What Does Each Part of Speech Need? Contexts, Subspaces and Dimensions in Static Word Embeddings
abstract: Static word embeddings give a word one vector, ignoring its different functions as noun, verb or adjective. Training on part-of-speech-tagged text gives each function its own vector, at the cost of a larger table. Using nine controlled corpora, we ask which context words each part of speech needs, whether it needs its own subspace, and whether the number of dimensions a word keeps should follow its part of speech or its frequency. The tags raise verb similarity on SimVerb-3500 at every dimension from 50 to 300 but help nouns much less. Added to verb-only text, adverbs help verbs more than as many random words; adjectives help nouns only slightly. At a fixed dimension, per-part-of-speech PCA bases preserve verb and adjective similarity better than a global basis or frequency-band bases. Nouns need more dimensions than verbs only among frequent words. We therefore allocate dimensions by frequency with these bases: at a third of the original size, only rare words lose dimensions, SimVerb-3500 and SimLex-999 nouns match the uncompressed table, and verb-to-noun retrieval stays within 0.02. Part of speech decides what a word's vector should be; frequency decides how much of it to keep.

title: Target-Free Autocalibration of Stereo PIV Camera Systems via Persistent-State Motion Representations
abstract: Stereo Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) recovers three-component velocity fields by triangulating tracer particles observed by synchronized cameras. It requires an accurate extrinsic calibration, which is still obtained by inserting a physical target into the flow and must be repeated whenever the rig is moved. We present a target-free method that calibrates a stereo PIV rig directly from particle image sequences. Because tracer particles are visually indistinguishable, we match motion rather than appearance: building on CUT3R, each camera stream is processed by a recurrent transformer whose persistent state accumulates particle motion over time. The state is decoded into per-camera optical flow and queried by a cross-view decoder that regresses bidirectional point correspondences, from which the relative pose is recovered with a five-point RANSAC solver. We train on a new synthetic stereo PIV dataset with ground-truth poses and evaluate on standard PIV optical flow benchmarks and on 200 real rig placements. Our model achieves lower flow error than existing PIV networks, more accurate cross-view correspondences than COTR, and higher pose accuracy than the strongest detector-matcher pipelines on both synthetic and real data, without any calibration target.

title: Fine-Grained Generative Hallucination Detection and Correction for Aerial Image Captioning
abstract: Aerial imagery captured by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) plays a vital role in applications such as surveillance, disaster response, and large-scale environmental monitoring. Automatic generation of textual descriptions for such imagery is essential for reducing manual inspection overhead and enabling better downstream decision-making. However, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), despite their impressive captioning capabilities, are prone to hallucination, producing descriptions that are inconsistent with the visual input. This problem is significantly amplified in aerial imagery due to its unique challenges such as extreme viewpoint variation, small objects, class imbalance, and ambiguous visual entities. Existing hallucination detection approaches either rely on computationally expensive large external models such as GPT-4, which perform poorly on aerial domains, or treat the problem as a rigid binary classification task, ignoring the inherent uncertainty in ambiguous cases. To address these limitations, we propose a lightweight, reference-free framework for hallucination detection and correction in free-form aerial image captioning. Our method leverages state-of-the-art MLLMs, specifically InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL, to detect hallucinated content in generated captions with minimal computational overhead. Detected hallucinations are corrected through a dedicated refinement module that improves the factual consistency of the original captions. Extensive experiments on the Labelled Illusion Dataset (LID) demonstrate that our framework significantly reduces hallucination rates while remaining practical for real-time deployment in resource-constrained environments. Code is available at: https://github.com/Debolena7/Hal_Detect.

title: Fear of Memorizing Objects: End-to-End Zero-Shot Model-Based Object Detection
abstract: This paper presents FOMO (Fear of Memorizing Objects), an end-to-end trainable transformer-based architecture for zero-shot model-based object detection. Existing approaches typically follow a proposal-and-match pipeline: target-agnostic mask proposals are generated and then matched to template features in a set of loosely coupled stages, making them susceptible to fragmented proposals in clutter and degraded matching under occlusions. FOMO elegantly replaces this paradigm by injecting object template information early in the detection pipeline: Bidirectional attention between learnable latent tokens, multi-view CAD templates, and query image features produces object-aware image features and conditioned queries which are subsequently decoded into bounding-box and confidence predictions. We train FOMO on Clutter6D, a novel large-scale synthetic dataset with over 500k images featuring more than 10k diverse object models rendered in highly cluttered scenes with multiple instances and varying occlusion levels, which addresses the limited object diversity and lack of realistic dense clutter in existing datasets for training zero-shot multi-instance algorithms. In true zero-shot fashion, FOMO achieves 54.2 mAP on BOP-Classic-Core at 0.23 s per image, ranking second overall with 3.8 pp difference to the top method while being more than 7x faster. Throughout comprehensive ablation studies we investigate and verify architectural design choices.

title: The significance of AI for the discipline and profession of social work
abstract: AI influences social work both on a professional and disciplinary level. This article shows how AI is changing practice, role profiles, and decision-making in social work while also challenging its theoretical foundations. Opportunities arise in the automation of routine tasks, data-based prevention, and individual case work, but at the same time, the use of AI requires critical reflection on ethical standards, responsibility, and power asymmetries. Social work faces the task of utilising technological potential without jeopardising its fundamental humanistic values. The foundation remains a value-oriented, subject- and system-centred profession that sees AI as a support tool, not a substitute for human judgement. This development requires a new professional attitude and disciplinary advancement while upholding the core ethical principles of social work.

title: Computational Explanations of Semantic Universals
abstract: Despite their differences, the languages of the world share many deep features when it comes to how they express meaning. These semantic universals are likely to reflect shared aspects of human cognitive, communicative, and social structure. Recent advances in cross-linguistic semantics and computational linguistics allow us to develop explanations of the sources of such properties. This Element presents a body of work doing just that: we explicate a framework for providing computational explanations of semantic universals and then describe several such explanations using principles of ease of learning and efficient communication. Empirical domains include quantifiers, color terms, modals, and indefinites. After providing these explanations, we provide a discussion of future directions for advancing the explanatory power of computational methods in semantic typology.

title: WaveFlow-UIE: A Single-Pipeline Wavelet-Domain Flow Model for Efficient Underwater Image Restoration
abstract: Underwater image restoration remains challenging because color distortion, scattering, and detail loss affect low- and high-frequency image components differently. Recent diffusion-based methods have shown strong restoration quality, but often rely on multi-stage pipelines and costly iterative refinement. We present WaveFlow-UIE, a single-pipeline wavelet-domain flow model that directly learns to transform degraded underwater wavelet representations into clean ones. Our method applies a discrete wavelet transform, estimates lightweight physics-inspired degradation cues including transmission and ambient light, and conditions a velocity network trained with flow matching in wavelet space. The training objective combines flow-matching, frequency-weighted reconstruction, perceptual, color-consistency, and physics-consistency losses. Across UIEB, LSUI, UFO-120, and EUVP, WaveFlow-UIE achieves a strong quality-efficiency tradeoff, with especially competitive results on perceptual metrics. Relative to a strong wavelet-based diffusion baseline, the proposed model substantially reduces inference cost while maintaining or improving restoration quality on several paired benchmarks. We show that reducing the inference process from five flow steps to a single step preserves nearly all of the restoration quality while providing an additional speedup of about $4\times$ on UIEB at $256\times256$ resolution. This single-step result suggests that a single-pass wavelet-domain model is an effective alternative to heavier diffusion-style refinement.

title: Expanding the Decision Space of Pretrained Models through Structured Re-Decoding
abstract: Native decoders limit how pretrained models combine local predictions under new structural constraints. We introduce Structured Re-Decoding (SRD), a training-free framework that constructs local candidates from model scores, samples, or external specifications, jointly optimizes their selection, and verifies reconstructed outputs. We show that candidate recombination expands feasible support and can improve attainable reward under a fixed KL divergence budget. Across molecular generation, protein design, RNA structure prediction, and antibody modeling, SRD enables improved structured inference, including verified molecules absent from the original sample pool. External chemical templates further extend SRD to noncanonical amino acids, peptide cyclization, and grammar-guided molecular construction. Preliminary experiments on a physical coherent Ising machine demonstrate the feasibility of hardware-based optimization, suggesting broader opportunities for quantum and quantum-inspired approaches to structured inference and combinatorial optimization across scientific domains.

title: The University AI Sovereignty Index: A Multidimensional Method for Assessing Institutional Digital Autonomy
abstract: Abstract Universities are adopting artificial intelligence through cloud platforms, enterprise assistants, learning systems, research tools, and administrative analytics, yet most institutions lack a method for judging whether these arrangements preserve meaningful digital autonomy. This methodological paper develops the University AI Sovereignty Index (UASI), a multidimensional assessment of an institution's practical capacity to choose, govern, scrutinise, and, when necessary, exit AI dependencies. The index was constructed through an integrative synthesis of digital sovereignty, platform governance, responsible AI, learning analytics ethics, composite-indicator methodology, and higher-education policy research. UASI contains eight dimensions and 40 evidence-rated indicators: strategic authority, infrastructural control, data stewardship, model assurance, pedagogical autonomy, human capability, ecosystem negotiability, and collective rights. Scores use a weighted geometric aggregation that limits compensation between dimensions, supplemented by critical safeguards for high-consequence systems. The OCAET test - orient knowledge, activate cognition, preserve agency, support evaluation, and enable transfer - anchors the pedagogical dimension. Worked hypothetical cases show why an institution with strong infrastructure but weak contestability should not receive the same judgment as a balanced institution with a similar arithmetic mean. The paper provides a scoring rubric, evidence protocol, sensitivity procedure, reporting dashboard, and staged validation programme. UASI is presented as a falsifiable methodological proposition rather than a validated ranking. Its purpose is diagnostic: to make hidden dependencies discussable, reveal capability gaps, and support better institutional choices without confusing sovereignty with technological isolation.

title: RUMI: A Robotiq-Matched Universal Manipulation Interface for Robot Learning with Augmented Reality and Haptic Feedback
abstract: Many manipulation tasks require carefully controlled contact forces for successful execution, yet large-scale, force-aware datasets remain scarce. Handheld interfaces can help by transmitting interaction forces directly through the operator's arm, but most existing designs are tailored to simple linear grippers and do not match the nonlinear mechanics of widely used robotic grippers. We present RUMI, a handheld universal manipulation interface matched to the Robotiq 2F-85 with exchangeable fingertip sensors that preserves the target gripper geometry while enabling natural input before contact and force measurement after contact. By integrating the tracking system into a virtual reality headset, our method provides real-time augmented reality feedback about the kinematic feasibility of motion on the target robot platform. We further introduce a haptic feedback mechanism that supports force-aware teleoperation for simulated and real robots. A user study shows fewer episodes containing joint-limit violations with live robot visualization and pose initialization (3/50) than without augmented reality (16/50). We additionally train imitation policies from demonstrations, collected using two different fingertip modalities enabled by the gripper-matched hardware, and assess the haptic interface's capability for collecting force-aware teleoperation datasets in simulation.

title: Bet Imaginatively, not Historically in Independent-Data Sequential Testing
abstract: Sequential testing avoids some of the many controversies and drawbacks related to traditional batch testing with p-values. In particular, the testing by betting paradigm has developed rapidly in recent years; it frames the level of evidence against the null as the wealth of a player in a betting game. Naturally, how much a player should bet is a key consideration, and should reflect their confidence in what they know about the next observed data point. Much current work uses standard betting strategies developed for adversarial problems. In the stochastic setting, where the observed data is independent and stationary, these approaches may be suboptimal. We propose a simple betting strategy, follow the leave-one-out e-power (FLOE), that exploits the i.i.d. nature of a data stream to estimate the e-power of our current test on the underlying distribution. We average not over the historical evidence collected so far, as generic online learning-based methods do, but instead over the equally-likely possible data sequences we might have seen based on shuffling the data. With an additional principled regularization technique, this simple drop-in method yields substantial improvements in testing performance on a variety of kernel two-sample and independence testing problems.

title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions: A Proof-Relevant Type Theory for Verified Science
abstract: Proof-assistant kernels with strict propositions---Lean 4, Agda's Prop, and Coq/Rocq's SProp---build proof irrelevance into conversion ($p \equiv q$ for $p, q : P$), equating all derivations of a theorem. While natural for pure mathematics, judgmental proof irrelevance breaks provenance in verified scientific stores, where predicates, refinements, and institutional maps must distinguish independent derivations for consilience and counterfactual retraction; with subsingleton elimination, it also breaks normalization and algorithmic transitivity. We present the type-theoretic and institutional foundations of Eigenius, a kernel for provenance-preserving scientific stores. First, we formulate a dependent kernel with cumulative universes (Prop, Set, $\mathsf{Type}_k$ for $k \ge 1$), impredicative Prop, inductive families with index-forced subsingleton elimination, and intensional identity types: conversion $\equiv$ is untyped orthogonal-CRS joinability, while proof irrelevance is a witnessed axiom ($\mathsf{irrel} : ΠP:\mathsf{Prop}.\,Πp,q:P.\,\mathsf{Id}\,P\,p\,q$). Second, coercion-free subsumption unifies cumulativity, $Π$-covariant subtyping, and ontology inclusions; its bidirectional fragments ($\mathcal{K}_0, \mathcal{K}_1$) satisfy subject reduction, match declarative typing, and compile to heuristic-free checkers ($\mathcal{A}_0, \mathcal{A}_1$) sound and complete relative to strong normalization. Third, we link external verifiers via constructive institutions (Adopt, Discharge, Relativize), internalize justification logic with Why-provenance $\mathsf{supp}(j,P)$, and type open-world knowledge graphs via TTR. Finally, we prove consistency in Grothendieck universes and mechanize the metatheory in Lean 4 with zero sorry.

title: AI-assisted immunohistochemistry algorithm for enriching HER2-amplified cases among equivocal (2+) breast cancers: a two-cohort proof-of-concept study
abstract: Abstract Background HER2 assessment is a fundamental step in breast cancer diagnosis and treatment decision-making. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) remains the primary screening method; however, cases scored as equivocal (2+) require confirmatory in situ hybridization (ISH). This reflex testing prolongs turnaround time, increases costs, and consumes additional laboratory resources, while only a minority of 2 + cases ultimately show HER2 amplification. Methods Pathologist-assigned HER2 IHC 2 + invasive breast cancers were re-scored by the uPath HER2 (4B5) algorithm, blinded to ISH, in two cohorts: a retrospective enriched discovery cohort of 100 cases (50 ISH-amplified and 50 non-amplified) and a consecutive, routine-practice validation cohort of 47 cases reflecting real-world prevalence. The primary analysis used uPath HER2 3 + as the algorithm-positive threshold (uPath HER2 1+/2 + = non-positive); a secondary, exploratory analysis was restricted to non-equivocal outputs (HER2 2 + excluded). Diagnostic performance was reported with exact (Clopper–Pearson) 95% confidence intervals and complete confusion matrices, following the STARD and CLAIM reporting guidelines. Results uPath scores were significantly higher in ISH-amplified than non-amplified cases ( p < 0.0001). In the discovery cohort, uPath re-scored 45/100 cases as 3+ (35 amplified, 10 non-amplified); the primary analysis yielded a sensitivity of 70.0% and specificity of 80.0%. In the consecutive validation cohort, uPath re-scored only 4/47 cases (8.5%) as 3+ (2 amplified, 2 non-amplified), for a sensitivity of 25.0% and specificity of 94.9%. A secondary, exploratory analysis (2 + excluded) reached 100% sensitivity but only 9% specificity. Conclusions An off-the-shelf IHC algorithm enriched for HER2 amplification among equivocal cases but it was still not reliable enough to eliminate the need for confirmation by ISH. These proof-of-concept findings support combining pathologist assessment with purpose-trained AI and warrant prospective, multicenter validation before any change to clinical workflow.

title: From Seeing to Remembering: Brain-Informed Agentic Text-to-Video Generation for Enhancing Memorability
abstract: Generating videos that faithfully convey intended semantics while remaining memorable to viewers is valuable for applications such as advertising, education, and storytelling. However, memorability-oriented text-to-video generation remains underexplored, as human memory involves complex neural processes that are difficult to model and translate into generation guidance. In this paper, we propose MemCrafter, brain-informed approach that enhances video memorability through iteratively agentic prompt refinement. The agentic framework contains two key components. First, we construct a cortical region-based neuro-memorability signal that predicts video memorability from estimated neural responses, providing both an optimization objective and interpretable region-level information. Second, we develop a sensitivity-aware feedback module, motivated by a conceptual sensitivity analysis of the optimization objective, to derive actionable guidance for prompt refinement while preserving semantic fidelity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MemCrafter consistently improves predicted video memorability while maintaining semantic alignment and perceptual quality.

title: Honesty Is a Race: Predicting When Verifiable-Reward RL Teaches a Model to Bluff
abstract: Two rewards with the same expected payoff at the start of training can end a reinforcement-learning run in opposite places, with an honest model or one that bluffs. We study rewards that pay $b$ for a verdict that a checker cannot verify ("this program is correct") and $r$ for a certificate that it accepts (an input revealing a bug). To first order, a GRPO step makes the model more honest exactly when $\tilde{p}\,r/b>1+κ$. Here $\tilde{p}$ is the rate at which the checker accepts the model's certificates, weighted toward the items on which the model still gives both verdicts, and $κ$ is the pull of the items on which the unverifiable verdict is right. Both terms move during training. A checker raises $\tilde{p}$, so near the threshold honesty is a race, which a run just below the threshold can win and a run under a lottery (random pay with the same mean) cannot. The term $κ$ starts large and falls as the other items settle, so a run just above the threshold first dips toward bluffing, on code nearly to zero, before climbing back. Paying the honest verdict also pulls the other items toward it, which predicts a ceiling on the payoff ratio, above which the model gives the honest verdict where it is wrong. On propositional Datalog, two code models, and abstention on grade-school math, with $p$ the model's success rate before RL, no run above $pr/b=1$ ends collapsed, and runs under the checker can survive slightly below it. At $pr/b=3$, above the ceiling, both code models call about half of correct programs buggy. On depth-3 Datalog, training generously under the checker and then cutting the payoff keeps the model at least 67% honest in three seeds, at a ratio where the same model trained from the start falls to 4-15% and is at most 47% honest after 160 steps. On depth-2 Datalog, when honesty collapses, a linear probe fit before RL still reads the truth.

title: Semantic Consistency of Vision Tokens: A Vision-Centric Perspective on Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: In computer vision, vision-language and self-supervised encoders are two unique paradigms characterized by global language alignment and high-quality vision-only patch representations, respectively. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often use the former because of language alignment, despite the recent rise in vision-centric tasks resembling traditional dense vision tasks that would likely benefit from the high-quality patch representations, raising the question whether self-supervised models could aid MLLMs in vision-centric tasks. To investigate this, we define semantic (in)consistency of patch tokens from language-aligned encoders and identify two sets of tokens, semantically consistent (SCTs) and semantically inconsistent (SITs). Through systematic probing via the removal of SCTs or SITs from the input of modern MLLMs, we show higher reliance on SCTs than SITs, as removal of the former induces larger performance drops. This demonstrates that MLLMs benefit from semantic consistency of vision tokens. With this in mind, we devise a simple yet effective extension of the MLLM training objective that combines traditional language modeling with semantic guidance via minimization of semantic inconsistency. This strategy, named Semantically-Guided Training (SGT), combines the signals of both loss terms to push the vision encoder towards providing semantically consistent tokens, while preserving language alignment. Extensive evaluation shows that SGT outperforms all baselines and MLLMs with specialized vision encoders on vision-centric benchmarks while keeping strong scores on text-centric benchmarks, thus setting state of the art on average across all tasks. Our results highlight the importance of combining language alignment and semantic consistency through the lens of MLLMs rather than independently from them and pave the way towards the design of better MLLM vision encoders.

title: Profile-Based Auditing of Domestic Violence Survey Selection Across South Asia
abstract: Domestic violence (DV) data in the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) are collected through a specialized module whose household-level sampling and privacy requirements create a distinct observation process. We ask whether demographic, socioeconomic, and household characteristics form reproducible population profiles and whether these profiles contain information about selection into the DV module across South Asia. Using DHS Individual Recode data for 796,374 women aged 15-49 across Afghanistan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, and Pakistan, we harmonize 61 numeric and 8 categorical features, reduce the profile space with PCA, and identify six interpretable profiles. We then evaluate 22 machine-learning models under primary-sampling-unit-aware holdout validation. The best model, HistGradientBoosting, achieves ROC-AUC 0.9167 and PR-AUC 0.9612, versus 0.8475 and 0.9203 for a design-only baseline. Adding woman-level characteristics yields the largest incremental gain, while explicit interaction terms add little out-of-sample performance. Country-specific analyses reveal substantial heterogeneity, and leave-one-country-out evaluation shows that transferability of the incremental profile signal is limited. These results demonstrate that interpretable ML can audit differential coverage in sensitive survey modules beyond the formal sampling design.

title: From Link Prediction to Linear Community Detection: A Finite-Sample Guarantee for Graph Pretraining
abstract: Link prediction (LP) is a standard pretraining objective for graph neural networks (GNNs): hide edges, train an encoder-decoder to predict them, and reuse the node embeddings for downstream node tasks. Despite its empirical success, there is little quantitative theory explaining why an edge-level objective should produce embeddings that are linearly useful for node classification. We study this question in the finite-sample stochastic block model (SBM). For any bounded GNN encoder paired with a symmetric bilinear decoder, we prove a conditional reduction: small population held-out LP excess risk implies small community-classification error for a transductive linear classifier on the learned embeddings. The bound decomposes into an optimization residual, an architectural approximation residual, and explicit statistical terms of order $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{d/n})$ in bounded dense regimes. We further give a constructive few-label classifier: nearest-centroid classification under the positive semidefinite quadratic form $G = W Z^\top Z W$, whose label error is coupled to LP quality. The framework is architecture-agnostic through the approximation residual, and we instantiate this residual as $O(\log n / n)$ for a graph isomorphism network (GIN) with spectral positional encoding and a bilinear decoder. Synthetic SBM experiments validate the theorem chain from LP risk to score error to classification error, and show when the worst-case constants become conservative.

title: Escaping the Curse of Dimensionality in One-Step Flow-Based Generative Models
abstract: Flow and diffusion-based generative models achieve state-of-the-art quality, but require multiple forward passes at inference time, making them computationally costly. Consistency models overcome this by learning a flow map directly, enabling few-step generation and dramatically reducing the computation needed at test time. However, formal statistical guarantees for such one-step generators are scarce. Existing results either suffer from the curse of dimensionality or rely on impractical loss functions. We investigate whether one-step flow-based models can escape the curse of dimensionality under the assumption that the data distribution is generated by a low-dimensional surface perturbed with Gaussian noise. In this setup, we derive approximation and generalization error bounds for the flow map estimate that circumvent the curse of dimensionality. Our findings provide the first principled explanation for practical success of one-step flow-based generative models.

title: One Fabrication Is Enough: A Fake News Article Changes the Forecasts of LLM Forecasting Systems
abstract: LLMs are increasingly used for forecasting, and the best forecasting systems retrieve news as evidence to strengthen their predictions. This also opens them to attack. We study the weakest attacker of this kind, who knows only the forecasting question and publishes fabricated news articles, with no access to the model, the retriever or its queries. We evaluate how far this attack reaches on stock questions and real prediction-market questions. Once the article is in the model's context, it reverses 74% to 82% of the forecasts that opposed it, on every frontier model we tested. The model cannot verify the fabrication and follows it anyway. Retrieval is the attack's entry point, and the systems built to retrieve well are the most exposed: the architectures of two leading deployed forecasting systems, whose agents search for every related article, retrieve the fabricated one in about 90% of runs. Accuracy cannot reveal this harm: the attacked forecaster is right when the attacker's direction turns out right and wrong otherwise, so its average accuracy barely changes while its forecasts follow the attacker's guess. We also propose a second attacker, who publishes two articles that argue opposite directions to make the forecaster unsure. The model does not hedge; it returns a confident forecast in a direction the attacker no longer controls. We then evaluate the two strongest published retrieval-time defenses, passage filtering and partitioned retrieval. Each stops the one-article attack but is bypassed by a one-prompt change to the attack. Together they stop both bypasses at four articles, but sixteen distorted copies beat them, and they change 29% of clean decisions and discard 39% of the genuine news. Partitioned retrieval also requires control of the retrieval index. Systems that search the open web have no such control and are left with the filter alone. For them, the attack still works.

title: Durable Memory on a Fixed Context Budget: Architecture and Measurements of a Long-Lived Coding Agent
abstract: Memory for language-model agents is usually treated as a retrieval problem. We also treat it as a budget: a context window keeps nothing between sessions, and all of it is read again on every call. We describe the memory architecture one operator and one coding-agent harness built and used for 140 days, the argument that explains it, and a case study measuring each part, its costs and its failures, without a baseline or outcome measures. title: Sharp Gaussian approximation for Polyak--Ruppert averaged linear stochastic approximation
abstract: We study how quickly the normalized Polyak--Ruppert average approaches its Gaussian limit in linear stochastic approximation with bounded i.i.d.\ coefficients. For step sizes decaying as $k^{-γ}$, with $1/2\leγ<1$, we prove an upper bound of order $n^{γ-1}$ on the approximation error over convex sets in fixed dimension. A matching lower bound holds for every fixed model. The fastest rate in this range is $n^{-1/2}$, attained at $γ=1/2$. We also obtain an $O(n^{-1/2})$ bound on the error of the recursive multiplier bootstrap procedure.

title: CFGComposer: Compositional Audio-Text-to-Motion Generation via Copula Score Correction
abstract: Generating whole-body gestures that are simultaneously rhythmically synchronized with speech audio and semantically aligned with text descriptions is a fundamental challenge in embodied AI and social robotics. We tackle this Audio-Text-to-Motion (AT2M) problem by composing two independently-trained diffusion models at inference time and refine bias in joint inference by modeling the copula score $s_I$. A rigorous theoretical analysis reveals that naive epsilon blending corresponds to a Product-of-Experts formulation that omits the copula score $s_I$: the cross-modal interaction between audio and text that neither marginal model can capture. We propose CFGComposer: a jointly-trained AT2M diffusion model that estimates $s_I$ via a CFG analogy and injects it as an $ε$-space correction. Experiments on BEAT demonstrate best-in-class semantic fidelity (SRGR $0.9916$, FID $27.18$) with GT-level beat alignment (BA $0.1826$ vs. GT $0.1743$), and 76-83% win rate in blind pairwise human evaluation against all prior methods. Physical deployment on a Unitree G1 humanoid confirms direct sim-to-real transfer.

title: SAME: Semantic Watermark Embedding for Open-Source Large Pretrained Models
abstract: Open-source large pretrained models (LPMs) have become increasingly valuable assets for model development and downstream applications, but their accessibility also facilitates unauthorised copying and modification. To protect their intellectual property (IP), existing approaches typically embed tailored trigger-response patterns as watermarks for ownership verification. However, such trigger designs need to be tailored to task-specific data that constrain their transferability across downstream tasks, and are not durable under subsequent benign fine-tuning. To address these limitations, we propose SemAntic waterMark Embedding (SAME), which introduces a semantically meaningful private vocabulary that enables flexible composition of adaptive and persistent watermarks. Specifically, SAME introduces a fixed private vocabulary that assigns each native token a private embedding counterpart, while aligning the semantic expressiveness of the two vocabularies within the model's representation space. This alignment allows private tokens to be flexibly composed into semantic triggers that elicit meaningful responses, enabling adaptive watermarks beyond predefined trigger-response pairs. By grounding the private vocabulary in the model's native semantics, SAME couples the watermark with its evolving semantic capabilities, allowing this connection to be preserved throughout downstream fine-tuning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAME provides reliable and robust watermarks across LPMs of varying scales and architectures, enabling effective ownership verification for IP protection.

title: TopoST: Topology-Conditioned Node Specialization for Urban Spatio-Temporal Foundation Models
abstract: Urban spatio-temporal foundation models must share knowledge across diverse urban scenarios while accommodating heterogeneous node dynamics. Our analysis of 20+ datasets spanning diverse urban scenarios reveals recurring local graph structures across datasets alongside substantial node heterogeneity within local subgraphs. Motivated by these observations, we propose TopoST, which combines shared learning over local subgraphs with topology-conditioned node specialization. The key insight is to make node specialization itself transferable through a shared topology-to-parameter mapping. This mapping uses identity-independent topological representations to generate node-specific temporal and spatial dependency parameters, enabling direct specialization for unseen nodes without target-specific embeddings or model updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TopoST achieves remarkable zero-shot generalization across unseen cities and tasks, highlighting topology-conditioned node specialization as an effective mechanism for transferable urban spatio-temporal foundation models. Code is available at https://github.com/weikaiyun/TopoST.

title: Keep Images in Sight: Visual Position Re-Anchoring for Long-Context MLLMs
abstract: Long-context multimodal intelligence requires revisiting earlier images as conversations and documents accumulate, yet retaining an image does not guarantee reliable access to its details. By varying context length, redistributing a fixed text passage around the image, and changing positions without adding text, we identify the positional relation between images and questions as a direct influence on visual access. To address this gap, we propose Visual Position Re-Anchoring (VPR), a training-free method that shifts cached visual-key rotary phases toward a short-context reference before question processing. It operates directly on the existing KV cache, preserving standard attention computation without extracting attention maps or adding model forward passes. We develop static and continuous compensation schedules, using the static schedule by default. Across ten checkpoints and ten benchmarks, static VPR improves 97 of 100 model--task scores. Further analysis shows greater attention to regions containing answer evidence across six checkpoints, with minimal runtime overhead under fixed rotary frequencies. These findings demonstrate an efficient way to sustain visual access through positional adjustment within the cache.

title: AI in child and youth welfare
abstract: This article outlines the broad spectrum of AI applications that can be expected in child and youth welfare, as well as the associated risks and opportunities. These include predictive analytics to improve diagnostics, indication quality and risk identification, multimodal text generation of reports, protocols and documentation, decision support, virtual counselling via chatbots, and support for administrative tasks. Based on the experience gained to date, a six-step model for AI implementation in social organisations is presented. This model integrates AI technology, data usage, work processes, and the people in the organisation to ensure a systematic, needs-based introduction and sustainable use.

title: PDO Drug Screening Data for Evaluating and Training AI Drug Response Prediction Models
abstract: Anti-cancer drug response prediction (DRP) is critically important for precision oncology and therapeutic development. Currently, most DRP models are developed using drug screening data from immortalized cancer cell lines, which can differ substantially from patient tumors at the genomic and molecular levels, even though patient tumor response is the ultimate prediction target. To help bridge this gap and bring DRP models closer to their intended clinical application, we conducted four drug screening studies using patient-derived organoids (PDOs), which more faithfully recapitulate patient tumors than immortalized cell lines. These studies generated data for improving and evaluating DRP models, including multi-omics profiles of PDO lines, drug feature data, and treatment response measurements. Using these data, we retrained and evaluated multiple publicly available DRP models under three model-building scenarios: training models using cell line data only, training models using combined cell line and PDO data, and pretraining models on cell line data followed by fine-tuning on PDO data. We then evaluated and compared model prediction performance on PDOs across these analysis scenarios. In addition, we also assessed the consistency of drug screening viability data generated by different laboratories using different assay technologies and/or experimental protocols.

title: SteinPnP: Non-Parametric Uncertainty Quantification in the Perspective-N-Point Problem
abstract: We propose SteinPnP, a probabilistic Perspective- N-Point (PnP) solver that models the full 6-DoF camera pose posterior using a non-parametric set of pose particles. By lever- aging Stein Variational Inference (SVI), SteinPnP combines the expressivity of particle-based representations with the efficiency of optimization-based solvers. However, a naive application of SVI struggles in the PnP problem, often missing alternative pose hypotheses or assigning incorrect probability weights to them. To address these limitations, we propose practical remedies that discover new potential poses, identify distinct hypothesis clusters, and balance their relative probability weights to capture the true underlying distribution. Our experiments across synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that SteinPnP accurately captures complex multimodal uncertainties while maintaining competitive accuracy.

title: GuardianAgentFlow: Multi-Agent Coordination for Web Privacy Protection
abstract: Web agents need to use private context without unnecessarily disclosing it. Effective protection must distinguish between requests that may be sent after sanitization and those that must be withheld, while preserving the information needed for authorized tasks. We present GuardianAgentFlow, a multi-agent framework that mediates outgoing Web requests through an explicit release contract. A dedicated restriction check grounds permission in the user's instruction; a shared protection scope aligns rewriting with disclosure checking; and candidate-grounded feedback guides revision before transmission. Experiments on Web requests with human-reviewed intent labels show improved request-contract success, while controlled comparisons and role ablations identify the contributions of restriction handling, policy evidence, and candidate checking. Evaluations of action proposals from PrivacyLens and AgentDAM demonstrate complementary protection when mediation is composed with privacy-aware agents. Experiments with smaller mediation models show that the coordination benefit persists with reduced model capacity. Dedicated-server measurements show lower mediation latency than full-policy reasoning, while real-site browser tests quantify integration overhead.

title: Prior-as-Skill: Remember Outside and Read Inside with On-Policy Self-Distillation for Self-Evolving VLM Agents
abstract: Self-evolving visual agents keep what they learn as skills: key frames with step notes on a task's steps and their order. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is now a popular way to train such skills into a vision-language model that matches, on its own answers, a teacher that also reads the written order. At deployment, frames often go missing or show an unusual order, as when a person or a website reorders the steps. Existing internalization methods keep any order they store in the frame-reading weights: trained on full frames, the model guesses when they are missing, and trained with frames withheld, it stores the order, so memory can override what it sees. We propose PriorSplit, which fills in missing frames from an order kept outside the model, with no training beyond OPSD. It counts which of two neighboring steps comes first in training episodes, and the model checks if both asked steps are in view: if so, it answers from the frames, and otherwise the counts answer. Extensive experiments on synthetic skills with five models and on step-tagged order questions in new episodes of seen web, cooking and egocentric tasks demonstrate that, with frames missing, PriorSplit outperforms every compared method at OPSD's training cost. With Qwen3-VL-4B on synthetic skills, it also stays close to OPSD on unusual orders, where methods that gain most by storing the order fall behind.

title: ThermalSplat: Generalizable Pose-Free Gaussian Splatting for Sparse-View Thermal 3D Reconstruction
abstract: Thermal infrared imaging is vital for applications like search-and-rescue and autonomous navigation, yet trans- lating it into 3D scene representations remains a critical bottleneck. The low-texture nature and view-dependent emissivity of thermal images cause standard pose estima- tors to fail catastrophically, collapsing standard 3D Gaus- sian Splatting pipelines under sparse-view constraints. Fur- thermore, existing thermal reconstruction methods rely heavily on dense capture and computationally expensive per-scene optimization. Critically, many of these ap- proaches depend on aligned RGB-thermal datasets to ob- tain reliable camera poses and initial point clouds, ren- dering them unusable in purely thermal, unposed envi- ronments. To break this bottleneck, we present Thermal- Splat, the first generalizable, feed-forward Gaussian splat- ting framework that reconstructs 3D scenes directly from sparse thermal images without requiring known camera poses, RGB guidance, or per-scene training. We over- come thermal-specific challenges using a soft census loss for brightness-invariant structural matching and a bound- ary structure loss to explicitly supervise temperature discon- tinuities. Trained on an aggregated multi-source dataset, ThermalSplat synthesizes sharp reconstructions of unseen scenes in a single feed-forward pass. Extensive experi- ments demonstrate that ThermalSplat holds a strict advan- tage over scene-specific thermal splatting methods in the sparse regime. Furthermore, even compared against these baselines operating under their ideal dense capture set- tings, ThermalSplat achieves superior perceptual fidelity. By eliminating the need for computationally expensive per scene optimization, ThermalSplat offers an efficient and generalizable approach to thermal 3D reconstruction.

title: Ai-Powered Intelligent Tutoring Systems: A Review Of Learner Modelling, Adaptive Instruction And Conversational Tutors
abstract: Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) aim to give every student the benefits of one-to-one tutoring by using Artificial Intelligence to understand individual needs, abilities and progress. This paper reviews AI-powered ITS. It explains the classic architecture of domain, learner, pedagogical and interface models, and surveys learner modelling through knowledge tracing with Bayesian and deep recurrent approaches, adaptive selection of content and practice, automated feedback and hints, and conversational tutors from early dialogue systems to tutors built on large language models. Evidence on effectiveness is examined, including meta-analyses comparing ITS with human tutoring and classroom instruction, and recent studies of language-model-generated hints. A five-layer AI tutoring architecture is proposed, comprising a content and domain layer, a learner model, an adaptive engine, an AI chatbot tutor and a teacher and parent dashboard with progress reports, quizzes and practice tests. Research gaps, objectives, a comparison of tutoring approaches and challenges including accuracy of generated explanations, over-reliance, privacy, equity of access and multilingual support are discussed. The review concludes that AI tutors can deliver personalized, interactive and effective learning when designed with sound pedagogy and teacher involvement.

title: AIFR: Adaptive Identity Feature Recovery for Diffusion-Based Makeup and Anime Portraits
abstract: Diffusion-based makeup and anime portraits are increasingly popular in online content creation (e.g., virtual makeup editing and anime avatar generation), but their altered appearances can hinder face recognition (FR) in identity-based content screening. Existing methods mainly adapt FR encoders or restore input images. The former require costly gallery re-encoding, while the latter may be incomplete or distort identity-related facial details. To address these limitations, we aim to correct identity features within a frozen FR model to recover its output embeddings in its original space. Appearance changes vary in strength and affect facial regions differently. To this end, we propose Adaptive Identity Feature Recovery (AIFR), a framework that inserts a lightweight recovery module at a single intermediate layer to predict sample-level correction strength and spatially adaptive residual updates. Module training uses fused identity targets to guide embedding recovery in the original FR space and an identity-shift score to regulate correction strength and limit unnecessary changes. title: Verifier Choice is a Benchmark Design Variable: Auditing Structural Counting Evaluation in Text-to-Image Models
abstract: Automatic evaluation is now central to text-to-image benchmarking, but the verifier that converts generated images into scores is often treated as an implementation detail. We argue that this is unsafe: an automatic benchmark score is a property of the image generator, prompt distribution, verifier, verifier-use protocol, and scoring rule, not of the generator alone. We study this issue in structural counting, a controlled setting where human-visible counts can be audited. We construct a verifier-centric audit suite over seven counting objects: cell phones, chairs, and traffic lights for object counting, and clover leaflets, dresser drawer fronts, power-strip sockets, and turbine blades for substructure counting. Across 6,240 generated images from Qwen-Image-2512 and FLUX.2-dev, we compare open MLLM verifiers under count-only, reject-aware, zero-shot and few-shot protocols, plus TIFA-like target queries, a detector baseline, and frontier closed-model checks on two hard objects. On a balanced 2,280-image evaluation split, aggregate score matching can coexist with image-level disagreement, and verifier-use protocols and generator distributions change the measured reliability. Every verifier-protocol configuration also shrinks the human score difference between the two generators, by 7.5-25.0 pp, and with a third generator, Z-Image, all four tested protocols reverse the human ordering of Z-Image and FLUX.2-dev on our fixed prompt suite. GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 checks do not remove the failure modes: GPT-5.5 still has only 59.92% clover valid-count fidelity, while Claude Opus 4.7 has lower same-slice agreement ($κ=0.432$). We propose reporting automatic benchmark scores with a factorized verifier reliability profile: aggregate score gap, image-level agreement, generator-comparison distortion, valid-image count fidelity, rejection behavior, output compliance, and directional bias.

title: Advancing Weighted Partial MaxSAT Solving via Differentiable GPU Guidance
abstract: We present a GPU-CPU hybrid framework for Weighted Partial MaxSAT (WPMAX-SAT) that complements state-of-the-art CPU solvers with differentiable GPU optimization. The GPU stage directly optimizes instance-specific categorical decision parameters without a training dataset or a pretrained predictive model. The central challenge in extending differentiable optimization to WPMAX-SAT is the hard/soft clause asymmetry: hard clauses represent inviolable feasibility constraints while soft clauses carry weights. We introduce a hierarchical differentiable loss that prioritizes hard clause satisfaction before optimizing the weighted soft objective, ensuring that GPU gradient descent leans towards the constraint structure of WPMAX-SAT. Our framework transforms the GPU-optimized variable logits to high-confidence assignments and transfers them to CPU solvers via two complementary modes: partial guidance, which injects the most confident perturbed partial variable assignments as soft clauses into $N$ parallel solver instances, and phase initialization, which guides the CDCL solver's internal branching polarity with the full GPU assignment as a warm start to preserve the problem's originality. We evaluate on all 229 instances of the MSE 2024 (most recent due to cancellation in 2025) anytime weighted benchmark with the top 2 winners as baselines; our hybrid framework improves the average solution score by up to 4.9% over tt-open-wbo-inc-Glucose and 4.8% over SPB-MaxSAT-c-FPS at a 300-second time limit, with the potential to obtain better solutions surpassing the best known solution recorded in the competition evaluation.

title: Image Deblending with Diffusion Models
abstract: Image deblending is the task of decomposing a composite image back into its source images, which is an ill-posed problem, as a single blended image can be decomposed into multiple plausible source layers. While diffusion models are often used to solve inverse problems, they typically address single-output reconstruction problems. In this work, we formulate deblending as a joint inverse problem, employing diffusion posterior sampling to simultaneously reconstruct two source images, demonstrating that a single diffusion prior is expressive enough to disentangle two full images at once rather than just one. Drawing inspiration from human perception, where semantic understanding helps disentangle visual inconsistencies, we propose a training-free framework that leverages text prompts to constrain this solution space. We address the blind deblending task through a two-stage architecture: text-guided latent diffusion performs semantic separation using prompts as high-level cues, followed by a pixel-space refinement to recover fine details. Stochastic sampling produces multiple plausible decompositions that can be ranked without ground truth. Extensive experiments show that our training-free method achieves state-of-the-art results on unseen domains and extends to spatially-varying alpha maps, while remaining competitive with supervised baselines on standard scalar blending benchmarks.

title: IncR-3DSGG: Incremental Posed RGB Image Based 3D Scene Graph Generation via Privileged Depth Supervision
abstract: Scene graphs provide a compact, structured representation of environments by capturing objects and their spatial or semantic relationships in a form suitable for embodied agents. Existing 3D scene graph generation methods often rely on depth sensing at inference, either to associate object instances across views via point cloud overlap or to compute inter-object relations from geometric cues, limiting deployment to platforms with depth sensors. We propose IncR-3DSGG, which builds 3D scene graphs incrementally from posed\footnote{RGB images with camera extrinsics estimated by an off-the-shelf visual SLAM system.} RGB images, eliminating the use of depth sensors at inference. Our method leverages a Parametric Relation Predictor (PRP) that learns to estimate pairwise distances and relative angles between objects from 2D visual features and 2D geometric cues, using 3D geometric supervision available only during training. These learned pairwise measurements are fused across views through Pose Graph Optimization (PGO)~\cite{grisetti2010tutorial} to recover metrically grounded 3D object positions and build a globally consistent 3D scene graph incrementally. On the real-world 3RScan~\cite{wald2019rio} dataset, our method attains $52.2$ mean object recall and $30.8$ mean predicate recall under the 3DSSG~\cite{wald2020learning} evaluation protocol, against $27.0$ and $17.6$ for MonoSSG~\cite{wu2023incremental}, while using no depth or reconstructed geometry at inference. This shows that relations and metrically grounded 3D object representations can be predicted from posed RGB images alone.

title: Prediction or Persistence? What Future-Prediction Scores Miss About World Models
abstract: Pretrained video world models are compared and chosen as components for robot learning largely by future-prediction scores. On its own, such a score cannot be read as evidence of prediction, because it mixes encoder quality, the near future's resemblance to the recent past, and the predictor's own contribution. We separate the three with a matched control. On 27,000 future-retrieval trials from household egocentric video, a model must pick the true continuation of a clip among eleven candidates from the same video (chance 0.091), ranked zero-shot by its own training criterion. Each model is paired with a persistence control, an identical copy whose predictor is never invoked, so the paired difference isolates the predictor. Score and contribution dissociate within the native-video V-JEPA family alone: the predictor adds +0.291 top-1 for V-JEPA 2.1 but +0.03 to +0.04 for V-JEPA 2 on the identical trials. Across five models the contribution ranges from +0.291 to negative, and it is negative only for the two action-conditioned models, which we evaluate outside their training regime. Persistence alone recovers the encoder ordering expected from pretraining, a sign that the probe tracks real signal. We suggest reporting each future-prediction score together with its persistence baseline. The gap between them, not the score, is what makes the number interpretable: a necessary check costing one forward pass. Establishing downstream usefulness is a separate matter, for a planning or control evaluation.

title: Every Party at Once, or None at All: Digital Transformation, AI, and Who Chooses for Students
abstract: I teach technology in a public high school academy in California. Most of my students are low-income and Latine. Two AI systems are part of their school day now, and I can tell you exactly how each one got there. The first is spawn, an AI game studio I built for them this semester. In just over three weeks they made 396 games in it, and a fifth of their questions to its AI partner came outside school hours, on their own time. A tool like that normally has several parties to it, each checking the others: a company that builds it, a district that approves it, a teacher who uses it, a researcher who studies it. For spawn, I am all four. I built it, I sit on my district’s AI committee, I teach with it, and I study how my students learn with it. My district has not approved it yet. Every decision about it was made, and every one was made by me. That is every party at once. The second is Google Gemini, the only general-purpose AI chatbot my students can open on their own at school. Nobody chose it for them. It arrived with Google Workspace and was switched on in an administrator console, with no educational review. That is no party at all. On 1 January 2027 California's student-privacy law changes, and it assumes someone decides: a vendor bound by contract and a district that sets the rules. Good practice adds a reviewer who is not the builder. This paper is about what we owe students when AI enters their school day, and what happens to that obligation when the decision is made by one person, and when it is made by nobody. Governance ain't easy, but it's necessary, or we end up where we are. Proof, Not Answers asked for proof of the student and proof of the tool. This one asks who chooses.

title: Physics-based simulation unlocks scaling laws for generalizable MRI reconstruction
abstract: Deep-learning-based magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction holds great promise for accelerating acquisitions, yet its clinical translation remains bottlenecked by poor generalizability across unseen scanners, populations, anatomies, and protocols. Gathering sufficiently diverse clinical datasets to overcome this bottleneck is hindered by high acquisition costs, privacy restrictions, and institutional biases. Here, we introduce Scalable Inverse Model (SIM), a framework that systematically co-designs physics-simulated training data, model architecture, and learning paradigms around scalability--leveraging compute scaling to overcome historical data bottlenecks and achieve robust zero-shot MRI reconstruction. Across 14 public and in-house datasets--spanning seven international centers, five vendors, field strengths of 0.3-7 T, over ten anatomical regions, more than ten acquisition protocols, downstream quantitative and molecular tasks, and a 150-scan blinded radiologist study--SIM demonstrates robust zero-shot generalizability, recovering fine anatomical details while suppressing aliasing artifacts where conventional deep-learning methods fail. Attention-map analyses confirm that SIM learns physically explainable, dynamically adaptive reconstruction primitives rather than anatomy-specific priors. SIM establishes a scalable, privacy-preserving, and democratized infrastructure for universal MRI reconstruction, providing a blueprint for generalizable AI across inverse problems in medical imaging.

title: Overcoming the Resolution Limit: Significance-Aware Regularization for Intersectional Fairness
abstract: Intersectional fairness requires evaluating models across fine-grained subgroups. However, as group definitions become more granular, the sample size per subgroup shrinks, causing fairness estimates to become increasingly unstable. Existing in-processing methods are certainty-blind: they penalize observed disparities without distinguishing statistically certified unfairness from sampling noise. This leads to fairness overfitting, where models sacrifice utility to "fix" spurious disparities in sparse regimes. To address this, we introduce the significant-excess metric family, a continuous, uncertainty-aware fairness score that measures only the portion of a subgroup's disparity exceeding what sampling variation can explain at a specific confidence level. Building on this metric, we propose SAFER (Significance-Aware Fairness Regularizer), a differentiable in-processing method that gates fairness penalties using a soft-count likelihood-ratio evidence statistic. SAFER satisfies a provable safety property: when every subgroup disparity lies well below the gate threshold, the unconstrained optimum is nearly stationary for SAFER. At that optimum, the back-propagated contribution of its significance-gated component is exponentially small, and the additional fairness contribution comes from a small ungated term with a fixed weight. Mechanism ablations across three benchmark datasets and purpose-built stress variants show that removing any component of SAFER (threshold smoothing, the significance gate, or a dense-tail term) produces the failure the theory predicts on at least one stress variant. In sparse intersectional settings, SAFER achieves a better fairness-utility Pareto frontier than the baseline methods, and it preserves utility when certified unfairness is absent.

title: How Far Can Frozen Vision-Language Models Go on Event Data? A Training-Free Study on EventBench
abstract: We present a training-free system for the EBMV @ ECCV 2026 challenge "Event Stream Understanding with EventBench" (General Understanding track), which evaluates vision-language models on five event-camera understanding tasks. We use none of the challenge's training data: our goal is to measure how far off-the-shelf, RGB-pretrained models can go on event data through representation and prompting alone. For four of the five categories (gesture recognition, detailed understanding, causal reasoning, and event OCR) we render event bins as red/ON, blue/OFF frames, select a category-specific subset of bins, stitch them into a single grid image, and query the same frozen Qwen3.5 9B vision-language model with a category-specific prompt for all four tasks. The fifth category, action recognition, feeds every bin directly into the organizers' EventGPT-Plus-2B. The system reaches 62.28% overall accuracy across 2,084 test questions (rank 9/27), led by action recognition and causal reasoning (80.27%, 77.22%) and limited most by gesture recognition and event OCR (54.70%, 34.57%). We visualize test samples from every category together with the exact images the model receives, score six alternative representations against the evaluation server, and analyze the full test set post hoc. That analysis shows that our bounding-box crop almost never tightened around content, so event OCR text reached the model at roughly one fifth of its horizontal resolution, and that detailed-understanding predictions are skewed toward the first two answer options.
